body:
Great post!!

I recall once reading that a journalist once described
TK's Manifesto as a "rambling" document.

Some TK critics where preoccupied that some other writer 
might thought of TK's ideas before he did. They were 
totally uninterested in TK's conclusions.

Disparaging remarks are par for the course for journalists
unless they are being paid off with campaign money.

...

I know several people with advanced degrees in Mathematics.
I asked each what they thought of TK, and all of them
described TK as a sick pathetic individual and a blemish on 
the reputation of Mathematicians.

But in each case they reached their conclusions
without having read the Manifesto. 

...

How many people are concerned about the destruction of the
natural world and the annihilation of much of the non human
life on the planet? Certainly not TK's critics.

You know ... the recent drop in the stock market is a good
example of the kind of destruction of peoples lives made
possible by technology. How many people do you think will
be declaring bankrupcy tomorrow, each facing a tarnished
credit history for seven years.

Yes ... TK might also describe the preoccupation of the market 
as a surrogate activity. 

...

Two months from now there won't be a shortage of techies
expounding on the virtues of the market.

em

TK wrote :

126. ... technology is a more powerful social force than the aspiration for freedom.




In article <8ddn4f$4dl$1@nnrp1.deja.com>,  <pyro1488@my-deja.com> wrote:
>With the talk going around about TK's supposed "envy" of others because
>he was not able to get laid or land a job as an engineer, and how it
>allegedly drove him to kill others, I thought I would share my thoughts
>on this.
>
>Recently I reflected on a sociology course I took a couple of years
>ago, and remembered there was a section in the book about social class
>inequalities and its driving forces.  Well, I thought I would take a
>peek into the book once again, so that it might give me some insights
>on the topic which I could contribute to this forum.
>
>One major aspect of social inequality is occupational prestige.  It
>would seem to me, that if TK was driven by envy of others, specifically
>the status or prestige they held, on a scale of 1 to 100 the occupation
>he had -- a college professor for a top-ranked university -- would rank
>less than that of those he envied, particularly those whom he killed.
>Furthermore, in order for the claim that he specifically envied
>engineers to be substantiated, not only would it have to be
>demonstrated that he did not have the capacity to fulfill this putative
>desire, but his status then should have (theoretically) ranked below
>that of engineers.
>
>I also find it interesting that those who downplay TK's occupational
>success, for the most part, have not reached the level of prestige that
>TK had as a Professor of Mathematics at UC-Berkeley.  One must keep in
>mind that he quit the job; he was not fired or accused of incompetency
>by his superiors.  Here is the chart.
>
>Occupation - Prestige
>---------------------
>
>Physician - 95.8
>Mayor - 92.2
>College Professor - 90.1
>Lawyer - 90.1
>
>[...]
>
>Stockbroker - 81.7
>Advertising Executive - 80.3
>Engineer - 79.5
>
>[...]
>
>Manager of a factory employing 2,000+ - 69.2
>Police Officer - 58.3
>Cashier - 35.6
>--------------------
>
>Prestige is measured using surveys of how people throughout a society
>rate different jobs.
>
>While it could be argued that TK might have a much different set of
>values than society at large, I have not heard such an argument
>advanced from our resident pundits.  For the most part, the criticisms
>of TK have come from highly socialized individuals who conform to
>social norms -- and have formed opinions based on these norms.  Thus,
>one can only conclude that such critics are foolish.
>
>TK directed his mailbombs at a wide array of people holding different
>levels of prestige.
>
>One such critic of TK is a man who used to post here, David Buchanan.
>I did a search through Excite's search engine and found a Dave Buchanan
>who is a CEO of a hi-tech company called Three-Five Systems.  This
>particular individual's alma mater is the University of Iowa School of
>Engineering.  I'm not sure if this is the David Buchanan I had an
>exchange with a year-and-a-half ago, but I'll draw comparisons between
>TK and this hotshot.  The University of Iowa is no Harvard (which TK
>attended).  Three-Five Systems, while a fast-growing company, is
>relatively small for a hi-tech company: its market capitalization is
>roughly 840 million dollars.  Microsoft's market cap is at about 500
>billion!  (That's about 500x bigger).  While CEOs are generally of well-
>above average intelligence, generally speaking they aren't the
>innovators within the company: it's those who work for them that are.
>One of the more common complaints about Microsoft is that they use
>their size to squeeze out innovative competitors.  Nobody ever said
>Bill Gates was a creative genius.  The David Buchanan who posted here
>estimated that TK's IQ was around 130-140.  He offered no sound
>argument for this claim.  (As a youth TK's IQ was measured at 160-
>170).  One must wonder if Mr. Buchanan is envious of TK for having been
>a professor of such a prestigious college as UC-Berkeley.  One must
>also wonder if Mr. Buchanan is envious of TK's work on boundary
>functions (a task probably beyond Mr. Buchanan's ability).
>
>While TK's income was not all that great as a professor, he
>nevertheless held a very impressive social position (in my opinion far
>more impressive than that of a *small time* CEO who graduated from a
>*small time* university).
>
>TK's inability to reach out to females is a completely different
>issue.  I don't care to tackle this issue at this time.  All I will say
>is that the small timers who claim TK was envious of petty, corporate
>engineers are perhaps projecting their own psychological problems.
>
>Cheers,
>Pyro
